Background\\n\\nThe platform runs itself up to Delivered, and everything after (reading the merge gates, merging, watching closeout, cleanup) is currently performed by an operator agent acting on the owner\\u0027s standing pre-approval. That works but pays a model to do mostly clerical work, and it does not travel: a future peer node that claims a task has no way to know the owner wanted it landed end to end. The flag moves that standing instruction onto the task itself.\\n\\n## Design rulings from refinement (Brian, 2026-08-29)\\n\\n1. **Deterministic code does the landing, not an agent.** Gate-reading, rebase-merging, branch and worktree cleanup, and issue closeout comments are mechanical. An agent enters only where judgment is needed (triaging review threads), and that agent already exists: the fix-session follow-up machinery. \\u0022Dispatch an agent to finalize everything\\u0022 in the original idea resolves to \\u0022the daemon finalizes; agents are dispatched only for the judgment steps that already dispatch them today.\\u0022\\n2. **The four-gate merge bar becomes code.** The bar\\u0027s scars (PR #50 merged on CI alone; PR #62\\u0027s stranded thread-fix push landing after the bar check; the PR #99 chained check-and-merge near-miss) are today encoded in an operator memory file. The fourth gate especially - never merge while a follow-up is alive or queued, head must postdate the last fix session\\u0027s completion - is exactly the rule deterministic code enforces perfectly and models near-miss.\\n3. **The flag automates resolutions, never waypoints.** \\u0022Fully automated unless there is a legitimate question that needs a human along the way\\u0022 is defined crisply as: everything that parks or fails today still parks or fails. The flag only removes the human from steps where the human today adds latency and nothing else.\\n4. **Rebase merge, linear history**, matching the project\\u0027s standing merge policy.\\n5. **Peer-to-peer forward compatibility.** The flag lives in the published contract precisely so it serializes with the task; whichever node claims it (this machine or a future peer node with the same owner) inherits the instruction to land it end to end.\\n\\n## Open questions for refinement\\n\\n- Whether this should ship as a boolean or as the third value of a per-task autonomy level (interactive / standard / full), given interactive task mode is building the other end of the same spectrum. the task reaches Done on the observed merge, the GitHub issue receives the closeout comment and is never closed, no Jira transition is ever made, and the task\\u0027s worktree and tracking branch are reclaimed\u0022,\u0022An unflagged task\\u0027s behavior is entirely unchanged, and h9k status and h9k task show both display the flag and its completion-condition settings so an operator can see which tasks will land themselves and what they are waiting on\u0022]},\u0022AgentContext\u0022:{\u0022hasValue\u0022:true,\u0022value\u0022:\u0022## Background\\n\\nThe platform runs itself up to Delivered, and everything after (reading the merge gates, merging, watching closeout, cleanup) is currently performed by an operator agent acting on the owner\\u0027s standing pre-approval. That works but pays a model to do mostly clerical work, and it does not travel: a future peer node that claims a task has no way to know the owner wanted it landed end to end. The pre-approved state moves that standing instruction onto the task itself.\\n\\n## Design rulings from refinement (Brian, 2026-08-29)\\n\\n1. **Deterministic code does the landing, not an agent.** Gate-reading, rebase-merging, branch and worktree cleanup, and issue closeout comments are mechanical. An agent enters only where judgment is needed (triaging review threads), and that agent already exists: the fix-session follow-up machinery. \\u0022Dispatch an agent to finalize everything\\u0022 in the original idea resolves to \\u0022the daemon finalizes; agents are dispatched only for the judgment steps that already dispatch them today.\\u0022\\n2. **The four-gate merge bar becomes code.** The bar\\u0027s scars (PR #50 merged on CI alone; PR #62\\u0027s stranded thread-fix push landing after the bar check; the PR #99 chained check-and-merge near-miss) are today encoded in an operator memory file. The fourth gate especially - never merge while a follow-up is alive or queued, head must postdate the last fix session\\u0027s completion - is exactly the rule deterministic code enforces perfectly and models near-miss.\\n3. **The flag automates resolutions, never waypoints.** \\u0022Fully automated unless there is a legitimate question that needs a human along the way\\u0022 is defined crisply as: everything that parks or fails today still parks or fails. The flag only removes the human from steps where the human today adds latency and nothing else.\\n4. **Rebase merge, linear history**, matching the project\\u0027s standing merge policy.\\n5. **Peer-to-peer forward compatibility.** The flag lives in the published contract precisely so it serializes with the task; whichever node claims it (this machine or a future peer node with the same owner) inherits the instruction to land it end to end.\\n\\n## Design rulings from refinement round 2 (Brian, 2026-08-29)\\n\\n6. **Pre-approval never means merge-on-PR-open.** The flag is a set of completion conditions the daemon waits out, not a trigger. The PR completes only once the Copilot review has completed, all other required reviews have completed, and the rest of the bar holds. The task carries the settings that say what \\u0022all required reviews\\u0022 means for it.\\n7. **A required human review means a separate human, and the owner\\u0027s pre-approval does not stand in for it.** Some repositories, and some tasks by their own setting, require a human reviewer in addition to Copilot (not in place of it). In that case the automation waits for an approving review from a human other than the node owner. The pre-approved flag is the owner\\u0027s approval of the pipeline\\u0027s outcome; it is never counted as the required external review. If a rule says the owner pre-approves but the PR requires a human reviewer, both are honored: the owner is not asked again, and the merge still waits for the human reviewer.\\n8. **Branch protection is read, not re-derived.** GitHub already knows whether a PR is blocked on required reviews; the daemon reads the PR\\u0027s own mergeability and review-decision state rather than maintaining a parallel model of the repo\\u0027s rules.
